analysis.one_liner: Strips the EPA's power to regulate greenhouse gases under the Clean Air Act.
analysis.headline: A bill to remove all greenhouse gases from Clean Air Act regulation drew 125 cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Clean Air Act's definition of an air pollutant to exclude carbon dioxide, methane, and other greenhouse gases, and would declare that the Act does not authorize regulating climate change. That would end EPA rules limiting emissions from power plants, factories, and vehicles. It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and died there without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that emit large amounts of greenhouse gases — coal-burning power plants, oil refiners, heavy manufacturers — would avoid EPA limits on their emissions and the cost of controlling them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large fossil-fuel emitters and heavy industry

how_it_helps.text: Removes carbon dioxide and five other greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act's definition of an air pollutant, ending EPA authority over them [S2] [S3].
Declares that nothing in the Clean Air Act authorizes or requires regulation of climate change or global warming, blocking future climate rules under the Act [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the health costs of unchecked emissions — more smog, heat, and pollution-related illness — and communities near power plants and factories would face the most direct exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: People living with pollution and climate effects

drawbacks.text: Removing greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act would eliminate the federal government's main existing tool for limiting power plant and vehicle emissions, leaving no substitute in the bill [S2].
The bill would also take water vapor, methane, and other gases out of the definition of air pollutant, a broader rewrite that goes beyond any single EPA rule [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings flow to large emitters in avoided compliance costs; the costs — pollution-related health harms and unchecked climate change — fall broadly on the public. There is no compensating benefit to ordinary people in the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power subcommittee, where it sat; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 5, 2011, by Rep. Marsha Blackburn with 45 original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on January 5, 2011 [S5].
Referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power on February 1, 2011, where it remained until the Congress ended January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that would have faced EPA greenhouse-gas limits are better off because the bill never became law, though only in the sense that the regulatory threat was already limited; the public's protections remained in place because nothing changed — the bill's defeat preserved the status quo of EPA authority.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large emitters avoided nothing new; public protections stayed

for.name: Rep. Marsha Blackburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 124 Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee and subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: Of 125 cosponsors, 124 were Republicans and 1 was a Democrat; no vote was ever taken [S4].

industries.industry: Coal-burning power plants and fossil-fuel utilities
industries.note: The bill would have exempted their carbon dioxide and methane emissions from Clean Air Act limits, saving them compliance costs while the pollution burden falls on the public.
Large industrial emitters would avoid EPA permitting and emissions-control requirements for greenhouse gases.
